articles.sourceTitle: Nvidia allegedly engineered scarcity by funding AI startups to buy its GPUs
articles.title: NVIDIA Allegedly Engineered Scarcity By Funding AI Startups To Buy Its GPUs
articles.text:
Following the departure of now-former NVIDIA CEO, Jensen Huang, a new report by The Wall Street Journal (via Wccftech) has emerged alleging that NVIDIA artificially inflated the ongoing GPU and memory shortage by investing in AI startups that would go on to buy NVIDIA GPUs and build data centers. The reason behind this was to maintain the perception of ongoing high demand and to move an oversupply of semiconductors from TSMC.

The WSJ report cites an August meeting between Huang and his senior finance team, including NVIDIA's CFO and acting CEO, Colette Kress, during which Kress pushed for a reduction in circular financing agreements, in response to which Huang allegedly lay into Kress, calling her a "deer in the headlights," after she had pushed to scale back NVIDIA's $250 billion deal with OpenAI. Jensen's push for further investment into small-scale cloud providers was seemingly in response to the changing tide that saw AI hyperscalers move away from off-the-shelf components in favor of custom solutions. The situation described in the report saw NVIDIA on the hook for an "avalanche" of GPUs from TSMC, for which it would have no immediate buyers. Part of the issue highlighted by Kress was also that these small-scale cloud providers NVIDIA was investing in could not afford to buy NVIDIA GPUs, meaning they, too, could be a financial dead end.

articles.title: The Claude Delusion
articles.text:
November 13th, 2026

Something weird happens to people who are successful.
They start to think they're gods.

Actually accomplishing anything is obviously no strict
pre-requisite of success.  And maybe it's not so much
"being successful", but rather "being rich".  How do
you become rich?  Some people are just lucky.  Lucky
to have a physical talent, lucky to have parents able
and willing to nurture your talent, and of course
quite often lucky to have been at
the right place at the right time1.

Being lucky doesn't mean they didn't also
work hard.  But even—especially!—the Paris
Hiltons of the world, the children of Hollywood
superstars, the crooks starting their corrupt empires
with "a
small loan" (or a share of an emerald mine) from
their fathers—they all
strongly believe that they deserve their
success and then conclude that anybody not as
successful only has themselves to blame.

This is especially the case for people in tech, where
for years and years being good at programming has been
equated with overall (and often: superior)
intelligence2, and those
illusory superiority effects then amplify rampant
Dunning-Kruger to quickly turn "I am good at
writing code, and with some luck, I managed to be
successful" into a train of thought that goes
more like "I am successful. Success is not random,
so I must deserve my success.  I appear to be a
genius, I've mastered coding, anything else is
trivial.  Ergo, I am good at everything."

Bill Gates, MD / PhD Biology

Let's take Bill Gates as an example.  Now, mind you,
Bill Gates certainly has accomplished a lot, and his
skillset and professional background includes without
a doubt a lot of computer programming and various
ruthless monopolistic business tactics.  In a
recent New York Times interview, he describes how
he evaluated OpenAI's level of progress
(emphasis mine):

And I was going down to see OpenAI on a regular basis
to see the work they were doing, and I challenged
them, saying: Hey, if you can read a biology textbook
and pass the advanced placement exam — getting a
perfect grade, which is a 5 — then you will have
proven that you are reading. That is, encoding
knowledge in an accessible form.

And so it’s six months before the public release that
Sam Altman, Greg Brockman and Ilya Sutskever come to
my house and demonstrate to me getting a 5 on the A.P.
exam, even on questions that I had made up that it
couldn't possibly have seen — very complex biology
problems. It was nearly perfect. So that was shock No.1.

Now Bill Gates surely has shown an interest in biology
and, through his work with the Bill & Melinda
Gates Foundation, has probably read a lot of articles
and research in this field.  But the hubris to think
himself a subject matter expert able to make up advanced,
novel questions in a scientific field outside
his own and suitable to assess AI's true capabilities
and then being "shocked" that it could
answer these questions makes my point.

Although, what really cooks his noodle is the idea that AI
can do what he used to do: write code.

And then late last year, when Anthropic's Claude
coding models got super good, I could see that they
are as good as I am — it’s significantly my most
developed talent, because I was obsessed from age 13
to 24 as to whether I could write code as good or
better than anyone.

That’s another moment where I went: This is
incredible. That the capability of doing long-running,
complex tasks has now gotten to the point that they
are superhuman at writing code and in finding flaws in
code.

Take note of the emphasis I added: the very notion
that something else could be "as good as I
am" is, first of all, hard to believe and
secondly necessarily means that it's
"superhuman".  That man is not lacking
self-esteem, no sirree, Bob.

Likewise, this is also where many of the tech bros
appear to be losing their
minds, and this thinking ("Anything approaching my
skill level is superhuman.") explains a lot about how
we ended up with both stories of ultimate doom and
human extinction as well as the utopian nirvana where
AI solves all of mankind's problems (well, all of the
billionaires' problems, which appear to
largely converge on pesky
mortality).

Revenge of the Nerds

For most tech nerds, being good at programming
computers was a differentiating skill.  It was weird,
normies didn't understand it at all, you spoke your
own language (languages!), you could make a computer
do things.  You understood how the internet
works, and anything that's not working was clearly
written by complete and utter morons, and you could
easily write this yourself in an afternoon if you
wanted to.

So now you've created a computer program that can do
the same thing.  Your mind boggles!  And it speaks!
It confirms you, it praises you, it tells you that
you're brilliant—clearly evidence that it is
infallible itself.  But now imagine if it was
better than you.  What at first seems
inconceivable then must strike fear and awe in your
heart, for you have created a powerful
monster with direction and purpose all its own.
(And you sure have consumed enough pulpy science
fiction to know that your creature is coming for you
eventually.)

"Can you imagine a Beowulf cluster of these?" was an
old Slashdot meme before memes were a thing.
But the notion of having an army of minions to do your
bidding has always appealed to the nerds looking to
assert their superiority, and thus we arrived at
"agents".  "Swarms" of "autonomous" "agents".

This narrative of agency conveniently also relieves
you of responsibility.  You didn't fail to properly
restrict a potentially malicious program you trained
to hack other systems with persistence.  No, the
"agents" went "rogue". You have summoned powerful
daemons indeed.  Daemons that can produce code faster
than you (gasp!), code you don't fully understand
(although of course you could, you just don't want to,
you don't have time, you have too much going on, what
with your homegrown heavily customized harness).
It becomes obvious quite quickly that this, then,
must be SUPERINTELLIGENCE.
Superintelligence that COULD KILL US ALL!

Finally got my agent harness set up just the way I like it.

Power corrupts etc.

I picked on Bill Gates above to illustrate the overconfidence
effect, but of course there is no shortage of much
more exaggerated
egos making bold statements outside of (or even within)
their purported area of expertise, reflecting a
complete and utter inability to relate to other
people.  To them, we're all just NPCs.

The more powerful people are, the less empathy they
exhibit.  This is neither
news nor limited to tech; dog knows there are
countless rich assholes outside of tech doing
asshole things.  But few outside the tech sector
suffer the same level of delusion, of
thinking themselves solely and uniquely qualified to
decide mankind's future, to claim to have birthed a
digital Prometheus, to boldly declare (and use as a
perpetual shield) a literal Deus ex Machina
to cure
all diseases—if only they could find the
time to prioritize that sort of work over, say, their
military
contracts.

Pretending to even remotely care about climate change3
while at the same time undoing "15
years' worth of greenhouse gas reductions" and then
listing
environmental concerns as a risk factor in your S1
is just the cherry on top.

If these are the new American Gods... well, je
n'ai jamais eu besoin de cette
hypothèse-là.

November 13th, 2026

Footnotes:

[1] The actual citation for "Bill
Gates went to one of the only high schools in the
world that had a computer" is "The
Psychology of Money by Morgan Housel;
Malcolm Gladwell discusses this in Outliers
as well.
↩

[2] The entire interview circus in the tech
world revolved around this notion of exclusivity
and brilliant jerks: "Google hires geniuses"
was an oft-repeated mantra in Silicon Valley, so
logically, if you were hired by Google, you were a genius.
(Yes, all >180,000 of Google's employees.)
This translates to the other big or
exclusive companies, and explains why
everybody leaving will always note
that they were always surrounded by the most
brilliant minds.
It's Inverse Groucho Marx Bias.
↩

[3] And hey, we really don't need AI to "figure out
how to combat climate change".  We already know how to
do it.  We just have to actually show any willingness
to stop it.  Unfortunately, that's also exactly where
these megalomaniacs get in the way.
↩

Links:

Discussion on HackerNews
Everybody's Lost Their Minds
"Winning AI"

AI unlocks Gödel's notebooks, said to contain hundreds of proved theorems
articles.title: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths | Mathematics
articles.text: The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.Albert Einstein presenting Kurt Gödel (second from right) with an award at Princeton University, where the two became friends. Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann Archive“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.Von Plato said he had started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team.In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature.“In a couple of days, I got to see a 650-page explanation of the workbooks. It had to be controlled page for page, but it’s basically a work that is impossible to do for human beings,” he said. “Humans read one page at a time and we tend to forget things. It takes us a year to read about 50 pages. We just are not able to keep in mind all the different parts.“The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up to This is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentafter newsletter promotionA microfilm image of an example of Gödel’s  shorthand from one of his notebooks. Photograph: Institute for Advanced StudyGödel’s incompleteness theorems revealed the existence of statements whose truths were independent of the system they were written in: that is, they could not be proved or disproved within the system. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal, the highest honour in maths, for showing the independence of two well-known mathematical statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice.Gödel reacted to Cohen’s Fields medal by saying that he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when pushed for a proof by his peers, Gödel was unable to reconstruct one from his notes.The first task von Plato set Claude was to discover if Gödel’s workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which would reveal that Gödel had been telling the truth in 1966. The answer came back: yes, almost. “He was just one step away,” said von Plato. “There’s one definition that Gödel got wrong, but he had the right definition two years earlier, and so the thought is that he would have arrived at the right definition anyway if he had just continued for a few months. For me, the architecture of his proof is just wonderful. It makes all of these results of set theory follow a uniform pattern.“What strikes me especially is that he starts from ideas. He’s not like someone who plays with formulas and hopes to arrive somewhere. He has very, very clear ideas, and then he’s methodical. Step after step he goes ahead and he manages to fulfil the aims that he has in this formal work.”Von Plato said that when Claude presented him with the reconstructed proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, he ran it through the proof assistant Coq, a program that verifies the validity of mathematical proofs, and it passed. Von Plato believes that had Gödel published his work on the axiom of choice, he would have won the 1940 Fields medal. “Maybe he felt that when Cohen got the medal, that that was something he sort of missed.”In further discussions with Claude, von Plato asked the AI model to extract all theorems in the workbooks for which Gödel either had a proof, had sketched a proof or had an idea for a proof. Claude found 663. When these results were put into Coq: “About 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired, meaning that perhaps the statement of the theorem had to be made more precise, or some assumption had to be added. About 50 were false, and this is no wonder. Gödel himself, when rereading his notes, would occasionally add a marginal remark: falsch! [incorrect] or schlecht! [bad].”Von Plato added: “I am sure that the continued study of Gödel’s manuscripts will reveal further treasures. The workbooks contain, Claude says, more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics that have not been found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. So this is one thing to explore. But there are many others. His physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory I plan to start exploring once I am finished with my present logic projects.”Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, Indiana, has not seen Claude’s reconstruction of Gödel’s proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, but said that if it stood up “it is remarkable and historically interesting. Although how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians.”Hamkins said: “The fact that there are things in there that resemble [Cohen’s proof] does not mean he had it. It shows he was on the path. You don’t get credit for work you don’t tell anyone about. But Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising that his notebooks are full of exciting things.”

articles.text:
Qwen3.8 - How to Run Locally | Unsloth Documentation

Skip to content

I'm here to help you with the docs.

For the complete documentation index, see llms.txt. This page is also available as Markdown.

Models

Qwen3.8 - How to Run Locally

Guide to running Qwen3.8 quants including Qwen3.8-27B on your local setup.

Qwen3.8-27B is a 27B parameter dense model Qwen, featuring vision and reasoning capabilities, a 256K context window, and runs locally on 17GB RAM/VRAM setups. Qwen3.8 excels at agentic coding, vision and chat tasks, and can now run via Unsloth GGUFs, NVFP4 and Unsloth Desktop.

Nov 11 Update: Qwen3.8-27B GGUFs now use Unsloth Dynamic V3.1 which improves average accuracy by 5-10% accuracy at comparable sizes including Terminal Bench, DeepSWE and more benchmarks. We're working on an even better version of Dynamic quants which will be applied to Qwen4 and future models.

Run Qwen3.8 GuideDownload Unsloth

Thank you Qwen for day zero access. Unsloth quants also include:

Developer Role Support for agentic tools like Codex

Tool calling: Improved parsing nested objects to make tools succeed more

Dynamic 4-bit Qwen3.8-27B in Unsloth Desktop

Dynamic V3.1 Update (November 11th 2026)

We're excited to release new Qwen3.8-27B GGUFs using our updated Unsloth Dynamic

V3.1 (preview) algorithm which improves Unsloth quants by 5-10% accuracy at the same size on most benchmarks and is the best in class for most tasks including coding, agentic workloads and general chat.

Most quants from 2bit until 6bit are updated. We found 3bit UD3 quants to do on par with UD3.1, so we do not update them. We are actively working on making all quants better!

We ran agentic benchmarks including Terminal Bench 2.1, DeepSWE v1.1, and general benchmarks like LiveCodeBench v6, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, AIME25 and many others. We used 256K context lengths for all agentic benchmarks, and 128K for the rest. We followed the same methodology for Qwen3.8-27B as DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next which also utilized our V3.1 preview algorithm.

Dynamic V3.1 Full Breakdown

Click below to see full details of benchmarking and more:

Click to expand Full details and breakdown

Exllama-v3 considerations

To compare GSQ-RCO and Exllama-v3, we had to exclude the token embedding layer from the x axis, as Exllama-v3 uses BF16 for it.

If you consider the full download size and total RAM usage for Exllama-v3, then adding the BF16 embedding table and including all embedding sizes changes the plots. Our main plots's x axis removes the embedding layer sizes from all quant providers. However on pure RAM usage and disk space usage vs accuracy, the below plot is the true reflection of actual usage.

We have not investigated why Exllama-v3 keeps token embeddings in BF16, but as the lm_head is still quantized heavily, the embedding layer might have "absorbed" most of the quantization damage from it. We would be glad to benchmark new Exllama-v3 non BF16 token embedding quants like using 8-bit for example, and see if benchmarks change.

GSQ-RCO results are misleading

For LiveCodeBench, GSQ-RCO showed Unsloth UD3 quants doing consistently worse than ISTA's. However we found the opposite - UD3 quants (our OLD quants) do better than ISTA on LCB on all sizes except the smallest. UD3.1 further improves on LCB as well.

We approximate that GSQ-RCO used a context budget of 96K, as that best fits the data for the runs we have. At 96K, GSQ-RCO does somewhat do better than UD3, but at 128K, UD3 does much better.

On another benchmark, for ISTA GSQ-RCO's AIME25 benchmarks, their quants reach 100%, 100%, 100% and 96.7% accuracy recovery. And they said our quants do worse.

Through out investigations, we estimate ISTA only did 1 trial - we did 14 trials, and we show on average the recovery rate is 93% to 96% - not 100% accuracy recovery. And in fact our UD3 old quants do BETTER on average than their quants on 14 runs vs 1 run of theirs, so we draw the opposite conclusion if you run the trials more.

We also checked and graded our answers using Math Verify Dynamic 3.1 GGUFs and also LightEval and we find exactly the same conclusions. We also tried greedy decoding (temperature of 0), and this could not get the 100% accuracy recovery ISTA found across multiple greedy runs, as GPUs themselves are non deterministic. That is why you benchmarks should be run multiple times. Greedy decoding is also not representative of real world use cases.

We also checked 96K (which is most likely ISTA's budget) and 128K, and our quants still do on average better.

KLD of Unsloth v3.1 vs v3

We did KLD for multiple domains for Unsloth UD3.1 quants and UD3 quants - we reduce KLD throughout most quants and most domains - we did not replace the 3-bit ones, as we found UD3 to do mostly great, and the accuracy recovery on benchmarks was not significant enough with UD3.1 to warrant an update, so we did not update them.

Benchmark details and setups

We follow the same procedure for all benchmarks as for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as well as discussed in Dynamic 3.1 GGUFs. We used temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, min_p 0, no presence or repetition penalty, preserve_thinking and xhigh reasoning for Qwen3.8-27B.

⚙️ Usage Guide

Qwen3.8-27B Requirements:

Qwen3.8-27B 4-bit quants work on 16-19GB VRAM like RTX 5080, 4090 or a Mac with 24GB RAM. Table: Hardware requirements (units = total memory: RAM + VRAM, or unified memory)

If you want to use MTP for faster inference, prepare to have 1-2GB extra headroom.

Recommended Settings

Qwen3.8-27B is a hybrid thinking model with different default settings for thinking and non-thinking modes. Extra high is enabled by default so if you want shorter thinking traces, you can adjust the thinking effort:

Instruct (non-thinking) Mode

Maximum context window: 262,144 (can be extended to 1M via YaRN)

Thinking Mode: temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, top_k=20, min_p=0.0, presence_penalty=0.0, repetition_penalty=1.0

Instruct (or non-thinking) mode: temperature=0.7, top_p=0.80, top_k=20, min_p=0.0, presence_penalty=1.5, repetition_penalty=1.0

💡 Thinking + Preserve Thinking

Qwen3.8 has Preserve Thinking which leaves the thinking trace from the previous conversation. This increases the number of tokens you use, but could increase accuracy in continued conversations. Unsloth has 'Think' and Preserved Thinking toggles for Qwen3.8 (see right):

Qwen3.8-27B comes with support for reasoning_effort, which can be used to adjust reasoning depth and control cost. These toggles are automatically enabled in Unsloth:

xhigh (default): for complex tasks demanding thorough analysis

medium: balancing accuracy and speed

low: efficient reasoning optimizing for speed and cost

To change thinking / reasoning effort in unsloth run or llama-server, use --chat-template-kwargs '{"reasoning_effort":"medium"}'

If you're on Windows Powershell, use: --chat-template-kwargs "{\"reasoning_effort\":\"medium\"}"

Change medium to your desired reasoning level.

Run Qwen3.8 Guide

You can now run Qwen3.8-27B in llama.cpp and Unsloth Desktop. Feel free to change quantization type.

Run in Unsloth DesktopRun in llama.cppNVFP4 GuideQwen3.8-2.4T-A95B Guide
🦥 Run Qwen3.8 in Unsloth Desktop

Qwen3.8 can run in Unsloth Desktop, an open-source UI app for local AI. Unsloth automatically offloads to RAM and detects multiGPU setups. With Unsloth Desktop, you can run models locally on MacOS, Windows, Linux and:

Search, download, run GGUFs, MLX and safetensor models

Fast CPU + GPU inference via MLX and llama.cpp

Search and download Qwen3.8

Go to Unsloth Chat or Model hub and search for Qwen3.8 in the search bar and download your desired model and quant.

Run Qwen3.8

Inference parameters should be auto-set when using Unsloth, however you can still change it manually. You can also edit the context length, chat template and other settings.

For example using Unsloth Desktop with the 397GB Qwen3.8 (-91% smaller) allows you to toggle thinking modes, allow inline canvas, web search and code execution and much more.

Dynamic 1-bit 397GB 91% smaller GGUF of Qwen3.8 2.4T in Unsloth Desktop

Serve Qwen3.8 with Unsloth API

You can use unsloth run command and serve Qwen3.8 via an API using llama-server runtime flags, including context sizing, GPU layers, threading, sampling, networking, and tool configuration. For more info see our API docs or unsloth start.

Unsloth is now ready

You can also do many other things with Qwen3.8 via Unsloth Desktop like:

Train models: Fine-tune text, diffusion, embedding, and more

Generate media: Create and train images, video, TTS locally

🦙 Run Qwen3.8 in llama.cpp

Download the latest version of llama.cpp. You can follow the build instructions below as well. Change -DGGML_CUDA=ON to -DGGML_CUDA=OFF if you don't have a GPU or just want CPU inference. For Apple Mac / Metal devices, set -DGGML_CUDA=OFF then continue as usual - Metal support is on by default.

To run the model in llama-cli, follow the code snippets below: Remember to change settings according to your use-case.

⚡️NVFP4

Like Qwen3.6, we’re also releasing new dynamic NVFP4 Qwen3.8-27B quants that run ~1.5× faster than BF16 checkpoints, with better performance and comparable file sizes. Run Qwen3.8-27B NVFP4 1.5x faster on 24GB VRAM. We also added FP8 KV cache calibration for 2x longer context lengths! NVFP4 requires NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs like RTX 50X, DGX Spark (see Qwen3.8-27B), B200, B300 GPUs. For older GPUs, our GGUFs work well! You can run NVFP4 quants in vLLM only for now (SGLang is not supported).

See below for previous benchmarks conducted for Qwen3.6 as well comparing to other NVFP4 implementations which use 16bit activations vs our NVFP4 activations:

All benchmarks use 1x B200 128 concurrency. Higher concurrency can boost 35B to 17,561 tokens / s.

For accuracy benchmarks we ran KLD and Top-1 agreement over Code, Chat and many domains. NVFP4 is consistency 92% to 97% accuracy recovery vs BF16

For accuracy benchmarks For Qwen 3.6, we conducted MMLU-Pro, AIME 2025, GPQA for FP8, BF16, NVIDIA's NVFP4 and our NVFP4s - we show our faster quants do similarly on all:
